To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dietary uptake of AGEs is in the range of 10–20 g/d, which is 10–20% of the daily endogenous formation.

(I) dietary AGEs are an important source of AGEs in the human body, (II) the contribution of dietary AGEs to the endogenous AGE pool depends on individual AGE levels, and (III) dietary AGEs have no or only a very limited effect on health-/ disease-related biomarkers in human studies.
the intake of AGEs in the diet of the average European adult amounts to about 10 kU/day.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of the most relevant dietary sources of AGEs, the quantification of the daily intake, the assessment of the contribution to endogenous AGE levels and the effect on health- and disease-related biomarkers in human studies.
the identification of the impact of AGEs in the human diet on the development of chronic diseases.
the question, whether and how dietary AGEs contribute, at least in part, to the development of diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dietary AGEs have the potential to affect human health but their impact is not yet clear and further research is needed.
the risk potential of dietary AGEs cannot be excluded, and that further studies are needed to provide more evidence.
dietary AGEs are not a risk factor for human health.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are no conclusive studies to date to prove the relevance of dietary AGEs for human health and disease.
there is no conclusive evidence that dietary AGE levels contribute to clinical outcomes.
the current knowledge does not support the idea that dietary AGEs are harmful to humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk potential of dietary AGEs is not only depending on their intake but also on their absorption, distribution, elimination and metabolism.
dietary AGEs are a minor contributor to human health.
the scientific evidence for a health impact of AGEs is still insufficient, but there are indications for an impact on the individual health status.
